# Archive: Woodworking Fixture Profile

*Synthetic fixture for the metacognition pipeline tests. Not a real archive.*

## Contradiction ledger

- L01 (Q03 vs Q05): "I never use pocket screws on anything that will be seen" vs "This jig has three pocket screws and I have never once cared." Resolution: register-dependent (never on furniture, always on shop jigs).

## Questions

### Q01 [joinery] [shop] [probe: forced-choice]
**Q:** Here are two identical toolboxes, one mitered and glued, one butt-jointed and pinned. Which one ships to a client, and why?
**A:** The butt-jointed one ships. A miter looks sharp until it sees a shop floor, and a pin holds under racking in a way glue alone will not. I would rather hand over something that survives being dropped off a tailgate than something that photographs well in the shop.

### Q02 [shop-safety] [shop] [probe: critical-incident]
**Q:** Tell me about a specific time a safety shortcut on the table saw nearly cost you something.
**A:** I ripped a narrow strip without the riving knife in, maybe four years ago, because swapping it back in felt like it would cost me two minutes I did not have. The offcut kicked back and put a welt across my forearm I still notice in cold weather. I have not run a cut without the riving knife since, full stop.

### Q03 [joinery] [shop] [probe: ladder]
**Q:** Why walnut over oak for a dining table?
**A:** The grain reads calmer. Why does calm grain matter? Because the piece should recede behind whatever sits on it, the food, the people, the conversation. Why should the piece recede? Because I build furniture, not sculpture, and a table that shouts for attention has failed at its actual job. I never use pocket screws on anything that will be seen, for the same reason: the joint should disappear into the function.

### Q04 [admired-makers] [shop] [probe: artifact]
**Q:** Name a maker whose work you hold up as the standard, and point to one specific piece.
**A:** James Krenov. There is a wall cabinet of his with a door that appears to float off the case, no visible hinge line at all. That is the standard: joinery so considered that a client never thinks to ask how it was built.

### Q05 [joinery] [shop] [probe: contrast]
**Q:** This jig on your bench has three pocket screws holding the fence to the base. You just told me you never use pocket screws on anything that will be seen. Walk me through the gap.
**A:** This jig has three pocket screws and I have never once cared. Nobody sees a jig, nobody sits at a jig, a jig just has to hold registration through a hundred cuts and get out of the way. The rule is about furniture, not the shop itself.

### Q06 [shop-safety] [shop] [probe: triad]
**Q:** Here are three guard configurations from three different shops. Which two share a habit you would call unsafe, and which one is the outlier?
**A:** The first two both have the blade guard zip tied open, one for dado work and one just left that way out of habit. The third has a riving knife with no guard but keeps the guard within arm's reach for anything but a dado. The zip tied ones are the unsafe pair. A guard that never comes off is being ignored; a guard that comes off for a specific cut and goes back on is being used correctly.

### Q07 [admired-makers] [shop] [probe: critical-incident]
**Q:** Tell me about a specific piece, yours or someone else's, that changed how you think about restraint.
**A:** A blanket chest I built early on, over-carved, with a beaded edge on every single rail because I could. A client asked me why the chest looked like it was trying so hard. I stripped the beading off two rails to show her the difference and she picked the plain ones without hesitating.
